content.title: About
content.content: Mozzarella is a semi‑soft Italian cheese made from cow’s or buffalo’s milk. It is known for its mild, slightly elastic texture and delicate milky flavor. The cheese is commonly used in salads, pizza, pasta dishes, and as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional mozzarella production involves stretching the curd in hot water, giving the cheese its characteristic fibrous structure.
The word “mozzarella” comes from the Italian “mozzare,” meaning “to cut off,” referring to the process of separating the whey.
Buffalo mozzarella is considered richer and creamier than the cow‑milk version.
Mozzarella is a key ingredient in the Caprese salad, paired with tomatoes, basil, and olive oil.
The cheese has a high moisture content (about 50 %), so it should be kept refrigerated in an airtight package to prevent drying out.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Mozzarella provides a good amount of calcium, essential for bone and dental health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality dairy protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B2 (riboflavin) and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lower sodium compared to many cheeses
items.content: Mozzarella typically has less salt than many other cheeses, making it a moderate‑sodium option.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Live cultures in mozzarella can contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience digestive discomfort after eating mozzarella.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Mozzarella contains saturated fats; those monitoring cholesterol should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: The cheese loses freshness quickly; discard it if it develops a sour smell or mold.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mozzarella can be enjoyed fresh, sliced into salads, melted on pizza and casseroles, or served with olive oil and herbs. For a softer texture, let it come to room temperature before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store mozzarella in the refrigerator in an airtight container, submerged in lightly salted water or its own brine. When kept properly, it stays fresh for 5‑7 days.

chicken-or-turkey-cake-patty-or-croquett.title: Chicken or Turkey Cake, Patty, or Croquette

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey cake, patty and croquette are ready‑made products made from ground poultry, shaped into a loaf, flat patty or small croquette. They are usually cooked by steaming, baking or frying and can be served as a main dish or used as an ingredient in salads, sandwiches and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken cake is often enriched with vegetables, herbs and sometimes cheese for extra flavor.
Turkey mince contains less fat than chicken, making turkey versions lower in calories.
Poultry croquettes are typically breaded with breadcrumbs or cornflakes, giving them a crunchy crust.
These products are popular in school cafeterias and as quick snacks.
In some cuisines chicken cake is served with teriyaki or sweet‑sour sauce.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ground chicken or turkey provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Turkey mince has less saturated fat, making the products suitable for lower‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Poultry provides iron, zinc and phosphorus important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Poultry is generally easier to digest than red meat, making it suitable for children and older adults.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared products often contain added salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can lead to growth of Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some cakes and croquettes may contain artificial flavors or flavor enhancers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat in the oven, microwave or skillet. Serve hot as a main course, in sandwiches, sliced for salads or as a snack. Pairs well with mustard, yogurt, tomato or creamy sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in the original packaging or an airtight container for 3‑5 days. For longer storage freeze at –18 °C; fully thaw and reheat before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Wine, dessert sweet wine is an aromatic beverage made by fermenting grapes with a high natural sugar content. It is usually served chilled and used as an accompaniment to desserts, fruits, and cheeses.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet dessert wines are often produced from late‑harvest or “noble rot” grapes that contain naturally high sugar levels.
Terms like “Moscato”, “Port”, and “Sherry” refer to well‑known categories of dessert wines.
Wines with high residual sugar can be aged in oak barrels, imparting notes of vanilla and caramel.
Sweet wines are frequently used in cooking to make sauces, marinades, and glazes.
In some countries, dessert wines are traditionally served with festive meals, such as Christmas dinner.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenol content in wine helps combat free radicals and supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Improved Digestion
items.content: Small amounts of sweet wine can stimulate gastric juice production, aiding the digestion of desserts.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dessert wines contain modest amounts of vitamins B1, B2, and B6, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: The alcohol content may be an issue for those avoiding spirits, pregnant women, and children.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: High sugar levels make these wines unsuitable for people with diabetes or those monitoring sugar intake.

items.title: Caloric Density
items.content: Dessert wines are calorie‑dense, so they should be enjoyed in moderation to avoid weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve dessert wine chilled (8–12 °C). It pairs wonderfully with fruit desserts, chocolate, blue‑veined cheeses, and light cakes. It can also be used in the kitchen for sauces and glazes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dark place, horizontally, to keep the cork moist. After opening, reseal with the cork and consume within 1–3 weeks to preserve aroma and flavor.
